title: Tax Bonus for Working Australians (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2009

divisions.question: That we are facing a time of great uncertainty is obvious.The spread of Wall Street disease has poisoned the world economy.People in Australia are fearful of losing their jobs and their homes. They fear the prospect of a future of uncertainty and diminishing living standards.Our Government had to act. Our elected leaders cannot sit by and watch a disaster develop. Urgent action was needed, and the Rudd Government acted swiftly to pump money into the Australian economy through a series of handouts to targeted sectors of the community.With the crisis growing, Kevin Rudd and his government have announced another incredible spending splurge. Billions of dollars to be pumped into the Australian economy in an attempt to counter the recessionary factors that are leading to an erosion of business confidence, job losses and a contraction of the Australian economy with the frightening spectre of a depression.In announcing the latest measures the Prime Minister demanded that parliament rubber stamp the latest massive spending package. He wants the package passed promptly and has urged the Opposition to minimize debate and get on with it.Well the Opposition has every right to take reasonable time to carefully examine these latest spending proposals.In fact it is the Opposition’s duty to do so.This enormous spending splurge will impact on tax payers for decades.Malcolm Turnbull and his team owe it to the taxpayers of Australia both present and future to carefully scrutinize these spending proposals before approving them.It may be unpopular to withhold money from the masses and Rudd and his spending team will harshly criticize he opposition for any delays. But let me remind Mr Rudd that Australia is a democracy, and our democracy provides for a series of checks and balances.Those checks and balances require that Her Majesty’s Loyal Opposition in our Federal Parliament question and scrutinize legislation when they deem it necessary and in the public interest. Judith Troeth The question now is that government amendments (1) to (6) be agreed to. Nick Xenophon During the division, one of my colleagues asked me whether Senator Sherry’s assertion that I had not discussed my amendments with the government was true. I want to put that into some context. With respect to Senator Sherry, I think his advice may be wrong. The amendments that have been circulated, which I am not seeking to move at this stage, were foreshadowed in my second reading debate speech. The substance and the elements of these amendments have been discussed with the government. I just want to put that in perspective. I am not criticising Senator Sherry as such. There may be a misunderstanding such that, technically, the amendments themselves were not shown to the government before they were circulated, but the government is well aware of the substance of the amendments. Any suggestion that the government is surprised at the direction I am going in or the intent and substance of these amendments is erroneous. Dana Wortley I take the opportunity to contribute to the discussion in this chamber on the appropriation bills before us. In doing so, I acknowledge that we have a number of amendments before us that will be dealt with later today. Those in this chamber have already heard, both during the second reading debate and now in the committee stage, that these bills are part of a suite of legislation that is crucial and urgent in the face of the financial crisis gripping the globe and its impact on Australia. The passage of these bills through the parliament would be an investment in our nation’s future. They represent an investment in our nation’s families, in the homes they live in, in the environment, in our roads and their safety, in our community infrastructure, in our schools and the education and training they provide, and in the jobs of our workforce and their ongoing viability. speeches.speaker: Nick Sherry
speeches.brief: The government announced a $42 billion Nation Building and Jobs Plan, including a $2.7 billion Energy Efficient Homes program for ceiling insulation, $14.7 billion for school infrastructure, $6 billion for social housing construction, and $12.7 billion in one-off cash bonuses of $950 each for families, students, farmers, and low- to middle-income taxpayers. The plan aims to support up to 90,000 jobs and boost growth, with a temporary increase in the borrowing cap by $125 billion to fund the deficit.

speeches.speaker: Eric Abetz
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the government's $42 billion stimulus package is reckless and will burden future generations with up to $200 billion in debt, contrasting it with the previous coalition government's achievement of debt-free status in 2006. He claimed the earlier $10.4 billion package failed to create the promised 75,000 jobs and criticised the lack of scrutiny and rushed passage of the legislation.

speeches.speaker: Michael Ronaldson
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the government's $42 billion stimulus package was ineffective and fiscally irresponsible, claiming the previous $10.4 billion package failed to create the promised 75,000 jobs and that the new package would burden future generations with $200 billion in debt. The speaker opposed the package, stating it would not stimulate the economy or protect jobs, and called for more targeted infrastructure spending instead.

speeches.speaker: Nick Minchin
speeches.brief: The coalition speaker opposed the $42 billion stimulus package, arguing it was ill-directed, too large, and would saddle each Australian with $9,500 in debt, while criticizing cash handouts, unproductive school spending, and lack of parliamentary scrutiny; they proposed alternative measures including tax cuts and small business support.

speeches.speaker: Simon Birmingham
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the government's $42 billion stimulus package was a reckless, panic-driven spending spree that would plunge Australia into $200 billion of debt, burdening future generations. They opposed the package, citing the failure of the previous $10.4 billion cash splash to create promised jobs, and proposed a smaller, targeted alternative of $15–20 billion focused on tax cuts and small business support.

speeches.speaker: Nick Xenophon
speeches.brief: The senator argued that the government and opposition mishandled the stimulus package by making it unnecessarily political, and proposed a four-point plan for the Murray-Darling Basin that would bring forward $3.1 billion in water buybacks, $2 billion in shovel-ready infrastructure, $250 million in stormwater projects, and up to $2 billion in new money for regional adjustment. They supported the second reading of the legislation but reserved their position on the third reading.

speeches.speaker: John Hogg
speeches.brief: Several senators declared potential interests in the legislation, particularly the tax bonus component, and one senator expressed hope that a road built under the bill might pass through part of North Queensland. The bills were then read a second time.

speeches.speaker: Joe Ludwig
speeches.brief: The government argued that the $42 billion stimulus package was urgently needed to prevent a technical recession and protect hundreds of thousands of Australian jobs, delivering $950 payments to low- and middle-income earners, families, and students, insulating 2.7 million homes, investing in school infrastructure, and expanding social housing.

speeches.speaker: Eric Abetz
speeches.brief: The coalition was ready to discuss amendments immediately but the government could not confirm any amendments or support for crossbench proposals. Senator Arbib argued the $42 billion stimulus package was necessary to counter the global recession, citing Treasury advice and support from the IMF and OECD, while accusing the coalition of delaying debate.

speeches.speaker: Eric Abetz
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the government was rushing a $42 billion stimulus package without adequate scrutiny, leading to a $200 billion debt facility with no clear repayment plan. They questioned the effectiveness of spending on insulation and housing, and pressed for details on how the debt would be repaid, the impact on interest rates, and the accountability of state-run programs.

speeches.speaker: Eric Abetz
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the government’s $42 billion Nation Building and Jobs Plan was urgently needed to protect the economy and jobs from the global recession, and moved amendments to reduce several cash payments by $50 each, including the single‑income family bonus (from $950 to $900) and the tax bonus for working Australians.

speeches.speaker: Alan Ferguson
speeches.brief: Senator Bob Brown argued that agreed amendments to the Tax Bonus Bill would save $435 million by reducing cash bonuses from $950 to $900, redirecting the funds to job creation, heritage projects, bikeways, community funds, and water remediation, creating an estimated 10,000 jobs without increasing the deficit.

speeches.speaker: Nick Sherry
speeches.brief: The government argued that its economic stimulus package was urgently needed to protect jobs and counter the global financial crisis, and warned that defeat would harm confidence and the economy. The opposition opposed the package, citing concerns over a $200 billion debt burden and future generations, and called for negotiation.
